claim: LiCre is a single-chain light-inducible Cre recombinase comprising the AsLOV2 photoreceptor domain of Avena sativa fused to a Cre variant carrying destabilizing mutations in its N-terminal and C-terminal domains.
source: LiCre is made of a single flavin-containing protein comprising the AsLOV2 photoreceptor domain of Avena sativa fused to a Cre variant carrying destabilizing mutations in its N-terminal and C-terminal domains.
evidence: The abstract directly states the composition of LiCre based on the experimental design and construction described in the manuscript.

claim: LiCre can be activated within minutes of illumination with blue light without the need of additional chemicals.
source: LiCre can be activated within minutes of illumination with blue light without the need of additional chemicals.
evidence: The abstract states this property, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b demonstrating activation within 2-5 minutes.

claim: LiCre displayed faster and stronger activation by light compared to existing photoactivatable Cre recombinases based on two split units.
source: When compared to existing photoactivatable Cre recombinases based on two split units, LiCre displayed faster and stronger activation by light as well as a lower residual activity in the dark.
evidence: The abstract claims this comparison, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 comparing LiCre with nMag/pMag and CRY2L348F/CIB1 split Cre systems.

claim: LiCre displayed lower residual activity in the dark compared to existing photoactivatable Cre recombinases based on two split units.
source: When compared to existing photoactivatable Cre recombinases based on two split units, LiCre displayed faster and stronger activation by light as well as a lower residual activity in the dark.
evidence: The abstract states this property, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3c showing ~6% background for nMag/pMag versus lower background for LiCre.

claim: LiCre was efficient in yeast, where it allowed control of the production of β-carotene with light.
source: LiCre was efficient both in yeast, where it allowed us to control the production of β-carotene with light, and human cells.
evidence: The abstract states this application, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing light-controlled carotenoid production in yeast.

claim: LiCre was efficient in human cells.
source: LiCre was efficient both in yeast, where it allowed us to control the production of β-carotene with light, and human cells.
evidence: The abstract states this property, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing LiCre activity in human reporter cells.

claim: The Cre/LoxP system consists of stable insertion of 34 bp DNA sequences called LoxP in all cells and expression of the Cre recombinase in some cells only.
source: For instance, the Cre/LoxP system (Van Duyne, 2015; Rajewsky et al., 1996) consists of two manipulations: a stable insertion, in all cells, of foreign 34 bp DNA sequences called LoxP and the expression of the Cre recombinase in some cells only, where it modifies the DNA by catalyzing recombination between the LoxP sites.
evidence: The introduction describes the Cre/LoxP system with citations to established literature.

claim: Cre recombinase modifies DNA by catalyzing recombination between LoxP sites.
source: For instance, the Cre/LoxP system (Van Duyne, 2015; Rajewsky et al., 1996) consists of two manipulations: a stable insertion, in all cells, of foreign 34 bp DNA sequences called LoxP and the expression of the Cre recombinase in some cells only, where it modifies the DNA by catalyzing recombination between the LoxP sites.
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism of Cre recombinase with citations to established literature.

claim: The Cre-ERT chimeric protein can be activated by 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen.
source: For example, the widely used Cre-ERT chimeric protein can be activated by 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (Feil et al., 1996).
evidence: The introduction describes the Cre-ERT system with a citation to the original work.

claim: The FKBP–FRB split Cre system consists of two inactive proteins that can assemble in the presence of rapamycin to form a functional recombinase complex.
source: For instance, the FKBP–FRB split Cre system consists of two inactive proteins that can assemble in the presence of rapamycin to form a functional recombinase complex (Jullien et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction describes the FKBP-FRB split Cre system with a citation to the original work.

claim: LOV domains belong to the Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) superfamily found in many sensors.
source: LOV domains belong to the Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) superfamily found in many sensors.
evidence: The introduction states this classification based on established knowledge of protein families.

claim: In the A. sativa phototropin 1 LOV2 (AsLOV2) domain, blue light generates a covalent bond between a carbon atom of a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor and a cystein side chain of the PAS fold.
source: In the A. sativa phototropin 1 LOV2 (AsLOV2) domain, blue light generates a covalent bond between a carbon atom of a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor and a cystein side chain of the PAS fold (Crosson and Moffat, 2001; Swartz et al., 2001), resulting in a conformational change including the unfolding of a large C-terminal α-helical region called the Jα helix (Swartz et al., 2002; Harper et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism of AsLOV2 photoactivation with citations to established literature.

claim: Blue light activation of AsLOV2 results in a conformational change including the unfolding of a large C-terminal α-helical region called the Jα helix.
source: In the A. sativa phototropin 1 LOV2 (AsLOV2) domain, blue light generates a covalent bond between a carbon atom of a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor and a cystein side chain of the PAS fold (Crosson and Moffat, 2001; Swartz et al., 2001), resulting in a conformational change including the unfolding of a large C-terminal α-helical region called the Jα helix (Swartz et al., 2002; Harper et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction describes the conformational change in AsLOV2 with citations to established literature.

claim: Each Cre subunit folds in two domains that bind to DNA as a clamp.
source: Each subunit folds in two domains that bind to DNA as a clamp.
evidence: The results section describes the Cre structure based on structural data from PDB entry 1NZB.

claim: Helices αA and αE of the amino-terminal domain, as well as helix αN of the C-terminal domain, participate in inter-unit contacts in Cre.
source: It was initially reported that helices αA and αE of the amino-terminal domain, as well as helix αN of the C-terminal domain, participate to inter-units contacts (Guo et al., 1997); and this role of helix αN was later confirmed (Ennifar et al., 2003).
evidence: The results section describes structural features of Cre with citations to structural studies.

claim: Cre mutants lacking the last four or more carboxy-terminal residues were totally inactive.
source: In contrast, mutants lacking four or more of the C-ter residues were totally inactive.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Deletion of the last 12 residues of Cre completely suppressed activity.
source: This was consistent with a previous observation that deletion of the last 12 residues completely suppressed activity (Rongrong et al., 2005).
evidence: The results section cites a previous study to support the observed results.

claim: The double mutant E340A D341A of Cre lost approximately 10% of activity.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we observed that a double mutant E340A D341A lost ~10% of activity (Figure 1g).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–37 of Cre, which entirely ablated helix A, eliminated enzymatic activity.
source: Deletion of residues 2–37, which entirely ablated helix A, eliminated enzymatic activity (Figure 1g).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Fusion of AsLOV2 at position 32 of Cre (LOV_Cre32) displayed the highest induction by light, with activity increasing from 15% in dark condition to 50% after 30 min of illumination.
source: Fusion at position 32 (named LOV_Cre32) displayed the highest induction by light, with activity increasing from 15% in dark condition to 50% after 30 min of illumination.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from testing various fusion constructs shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The construct corresponding to fusion of AsLOV2 at position 20 of the Cre A340A341 double mutant displayed a residual activity that was indistinguishable from the negative control and a highly reproducible induced activity of approximately 25%.
source: The construct corresponding to fusion of AsLOV2 at position 20 of the Cre A340A341 double mutant displayed a residual activity that was indistinguishable from the negative control and a highly reproducible induced activity of ~25%.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from testing fusion constructs shown in Figure 2c.

claim: LiCre generated more recombination events when expressed under the PMET17 promoter compared to the PGAL1 promoter.
source: At comparable duration and intensity (30 min and 36.3 mW/cm2), LiCre generated more recombination events in this experiment than in the previous one (Figure 3a vs. Figure 2c). This improvement likely results from the different expression systems and culture media that were used (induction of the PMET17vs. PGAL1 promoter).
evidence: The results section compares experimental data from Figures 3a and 2c and provides an interpretation.

claim: Two minutes of illumination was enough to switch 5% of cells with LiCre, and 5 minutes illumination generated 10% of switched cells.
source: Remarkably, we observed that 2 min of illumination was enough to switch 5% of cells, and 5 min illumination generated 10% of switched cells (Figure 3b).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 3b on the kinetics of LiCre activation.

claim: The nMag/pMag split Cre system displayed a mild but significant background activity in the absence of illumination (approximately 6% of switched cells).
source: Another difference was that, unlike LiCre, nMag/pMag split Cre displayed a mild but significant background activity in the absence of illumination (~6% of switched cells) (Figure 3c).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 3c comparing LiCre with nMag/pMag split Cre.

claim: Blue light exposure at 35.6 mW/cm2 for 1 hour is safe regarding yeast viability.
source: We observed no significant differences in the number of CFUs generated by illuminated and non-illuminated samples, nor between LiCre-expressing and non-expressing cells. We conclude that this light exposure is safe regarding yeast viability.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 3—figure supplement 1 on cell viability after light exposure.

claim: AsLOV2 has a fast decay rate of approximately 80 seconds for its adduct (activated) form.
source: We expected different response dynamics from these systems because AsLOV2 and VVD have different photocycle lifetimes, with a fast (~80 s) and slow (~18,000 s) decay rate of their adduct (activated) form, respectively (Pudasaini et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites established literature on the photocycle properties of AsLOV2.

claim: VVD has a slow decay rate of approximately 18,000 seconds for its adduct (activated) form.
source: We expected different response dynamics from these systems because AsLOV2 and VVD have different photocycle lifetimes, with a fast (~80 s) and slow (~18,000 s) decay rate of their adduct (activated) form, respectively (Pudasaini et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites established literature on the photocycle properties of VVD.

claim: Light pulses of 0.5 seconds occurring 10 seconds apart were sufficient to fully stimulate LiCre.
source: Remarkably, light pulses of 0.5 s occurring 10 s apart were sufficient to fully stimulate LiCre.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 3g on periodic stimulation of LiCre.

claim: LiCre outperforms the two previous split systems (nMag/pMag and CRY2L348F/CIB1) in terms of efficiency, rapidity, and residual background activity in the yeast cellular context.
source: Altogether, these results show that, at least in the yeast cellular context, LiCre outperforms the two previous split systems in terms of efficiency, rapidity, and residual background activity.
evidence: The results section summarizes the comparative data from Figure 3.

claim: DNA excision by LiCre occurred in a significant fraction of cells after only 2 minutes of illumination.
source: Excision of the target DNA occurred in a significant fraction of cells after only 2 min of illumination, and we estimated that excision occurred in about 30% and 40% of cells after 20 and 40 min of illumination, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 4e using qPCR to quantify DNA excision.

claim: The estimated frequency of DNA excision by LiCre was strikingly similar when measured immediately after illumination versus after 90 minutes in the dark.
source: The estimated frequency of DNA excision was strikingly similar to the one measured immediately after illumination (Figure 4f).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 4f comparing DNA excision at different time points.

claim: LiCre photoactivation was about fourfold more efficient in non-dividing cells compared to cells in exponential growth.
source: This revealed that LiCre photoactivation was about fourfold more efficient in non-dividing cells (Figure 4g).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 4g comparing LiCre efficiency in different growth phases.

claim: Expressing three enzymes (crtE, crtI, and crtYB) from Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous enabled S. cerevisiae to efficiently convert farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) into β-carotene.
source: Expressing three enzymes (crtE, crtI, and crtYB) from Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous enabled S. cerevisiae to efficiently convert farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) into β-carotene (Verwaal et al., 2007).
evidence: The results section cites established literature on carotenoid production in yeast.

claim: Metabolic burden associated with carotenoids production in yeast was shown to be substantial.
source: Consistently, metabolic burden associated with carotenoids production was shown to be substantial (Verwaal et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section cites established literature on metabolic burden in carotenoid-producing yeast.

claim: 72 hours after the light switch, the intracellular concentration of carotenoids in yeast had jumped from background levels to nearly 200 μg/g.
source: This revealed that 72 hr after the light switch the intracellular concentration of carotenoids had jumped from background levels to nearly 200 μg/g (Figure 5d).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 5d on carotenoid quantification.

claim: ERG9 is essential for yeast viability in the absence of ergosterol supplementation.
source: Given that ERG9 is essential for yeast viability in the absence of ergosterol supplementation (Fegueur et al., 1991), occurrence of the switch can be evaluated by measuring the fraction of viable yeast cells prior to and after the induction of recombination.
evidence: The results section cites established literature on the essentiality of ERG9.

claim: Cultures expressing LiCre were fully viable in the absence of illumination and lost approximately 23% of viable cells after light exposure.
source: In contrast, cultures expressing LiCre were highly susceptible to light: they were fully viable in the absence of illumination and lost ~23% of viable cells after light exposure (Figure 5f).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 5f on cell viability after ERG9 deletion.

claim: The highest fold induction in human cells was obtained with LiCre at 3.6 mW/cm2, with 5% residual and 31% induced activities, respectively.
source: The highest fold induction was obtained with LiCre at 3.6 mW/cm2, with 5% residual and 31% induced activities, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 6c on LiCre performance in human cells.

claim: The residual activity of Magnets-opti in the dark was very high (approximately 50% of switched cells) in human cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6c, the residual activity of Magnets-opti in the dark was very high (~50% of switched cells), which was surprising.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 6c on Magnets-opti performance in human cells.

claim: LiCre and the original nMag/pMag split Cre system displayed similar levels of induced activity at both low and high light energies in human cells.
source: LiCre and the original nMag/pMag split Cre system displayed similar levels of induced activity at both low and high light energies; they also showed significant residual activity with 5–10% positive cells for LiCre in the dark and 10–15% for the original nMag/pMag.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 6c comparing LiCre and nMag/pMag in human cells.

claim: The AsLOV2 domain likely prevents Cre tetramerization in the dark state because of its steric occupancy.
source: First, the domain AsLOV2 likely prevents Cre tetramerization in the dark state simply because of its steric occupancy.
evidence: The discussion proposes a mechanism based on structural modeling and experimental observations.

claim: The unfolding of the Jα helix in the light state may allow AsLOV2 to liberate the multimerizing interface of Cre.
source: The unfolding of the Jα helix in the light state may allow AsLOV2 to liberate the multimerizing interface.
evidence: The discussion proposes a mechanism based on structural modeling and experimental observations.

claim: The Jα helix of AsLOV2 and the αA helix of Cre may disturb each other in their proper folding so that they cannot exist both simultaneously in their native conformation.
source: Second, because the Jα helix of AsLOV2 and the αA helix of Cre are immediately adjacent, they may disturb each other in their proper folding so that they cannot exist both simultaneously in their native conformation.
evidence: The discussion proposes a mechanism based on structural modeling and experimental observations.

claim: The unfolding of Jα in the light state may stimulate proper folding of αA, and thereby allow αA to bind to the adjacent Cre unit.
source: The unfolding of Jα in the light state may therefore stimulate proper folding of αA, and thereby allow αA to bind to the adjacent Cre unit.
evidence: The discussion proposes a mechanism based on structural modeling and experimental observations.

claim: An important advantage of LiCre over split Cre systems is that it is made of a single protein.
source: An important advantage of LiCre over these systems is that it is made of a single protein.
evidence: The discussion compares LiCre to split Cre systems based on their design differences.

claim: The probability of forming a functional recombination synapse with split Cre systems is proportional to the product of the two units' cellular concentrations to the power of four.
source: Thus, the probability of forming a functional recombination synapse, which normally requires four Cre molecules, is proportional to the product of the two units' cellular concentrations to the power of four.
evidence: The introduction provides a mathematical inference about split Cre systems based on the requirement for four Cre molecules.

claim: Split Cre systems strongly depend on the efficient expression of their two different coding sequences.
source: Split systems therefore strongly depend on the efficient expression of their two different coding sequences, as previously reported (Meador et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study reporting this limitation of split systems.

claim: With an IRES, the two ORFs of split Cre systems are not expressed at the same level.
source: Although helpful, these solutions have important limits: with an IRES, the two ORFs are not expressed at the same level; with a self-cleaving peptide, cleavage of the precursor protein can be incomplete, generating uncleaved products with unknown activity.
evidence: The discussion describes known limitations of IRES-based expression systems.

claim: With a self-cleaving peptide, cleavage of the precursor protein can be incomplete, generating uncleaved products with unknown activity.
source: Although helpful, these solutions have important limits: with an IRES, the two ORFs are not expressed at the same level; with a self-cleaving peptide, cleavage of the precursor protein can be incomplete, generating uncleaved products with unknown activity.
evidence: The discussion describes known limitations of self-cleaving peptide systems.

claim: A non-cleaved form at approximately 72 kDa was reported for nMag/pMag split Cre in mammalian cells.
source: This was the case for nMag/pMag split Cre in mammalian cells, where a non-cleaved form at ~72 kDa was reported and where targeted modifications of the cleavage sequence increased both the abundance of this non-cleaved form and the non-induced activity of the system (Morikawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion cites a previous study reporting incomplete cleavage of nMag/pMag split Cre.

claim: Suboptimal stoichiometry between the two protein units was reported as a possible issue for CRY2/CIB1 split Cre.
source: The second benefit of LiCre being a single protein is to avoid problems of suboptimal stoichiometry between the two protein units, which was reported as a possible issue for CRY2/CIB1 split Cre (Meador et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites a previous study reporting stoichiometry issues with CRY2/CIB1 split Cre.

claim: Photoactivation of the original version of the CRY2/CIB1 split Cre can be extremely low.
source: We do not explain this result, but it is consistent with previous studies reporting that photoactivation of the original version of the CRY2/CIB1 split Cre can be extremely low (Kawano et al., 2016), and that the induced activity of the CRY2-L348F/CIB1 system can also be low and highly variable (Morikawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion cites previous studies reporting low activity of CRY2/CIB1 split Cre.

claim: The induced activity of the CRY2-L348F/CIB1 system can be low and highly variable.
source: We do not explain this result, but it is consistent with previous studies reporting that photoactivation of the original version of the CRY2/CIB1 split Cre can be extremely low (Kawano et al., 2016), and that the induced activity of the CRY2-L348F/CIB1 system can also be low and highly variable (Morikawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion cites a previous study reporting variable activity of CRY2-L348F/CIB1.

claim: The nMag/pMag split Cre system was validated as efficient by independent laboratories.
source: In contrast, we validated the efficiency of nMag/pMag split Cre and so did other independent laboratories (Morikawa et al., 2020; Takao et al., 2020; Allen et al., 2019; Weinberg et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites multiple studies validating the nMag/pMag split Cre system.

claim: The authors of PA-Cre3.0 reported that their strategy abolished residual activity and attributed this improvement to a reduction of the expression level of the transgene.
source: The authors reported that this strategy abolished residual activity and attributed this improvement to a reduction of the expression level of the transgene (Morikawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion cites the interpretation provided by the authors of PA-Cre3.0.

claim: LiCre displayed weaker residual activity than the original nMag/pMag split Cre in the dark.
source: In contrast, LiCre displayed weaker residual activity than the original nMag/pMag split Cre in the dark.
evidence: The discussion summarizes comparative data from the experiments.

claim: LiCre displayed higher induced activity compared to nMag/pMag split Cre, especially in yeast.
source: Importantly, LiCre also displayed higher induced activity – especially in yeast – and a faster response to light compared to nMag/pMag split Cre.
evidence: The discussion summarizes comparative data from the experiments.

claim: LiCre displayed a faster response to light compared to nMag/pMag split Cre.
source: Importantly, LiCre also displayed higher induced activity – especially in yeast – and a faster response to light compared to nMag/pMag split Cre.
evidence: The discussion summarizes comparative data from the experiments.

claim: The strong response of LiCre probably results from its simplicity since the activation of a single protein involves fewer steps than the activation of two units that must then dimerize to become functional.
source: This strong response probably results from its simplicity since the activation of a single protein involves fewer steps than the activation of two units that must then dimerize to become functional.
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation of the experimental results based on the design differences.

claim: The photocycle of active LiCre is faster than the one of active nMag/pMag split Cre.
source: Finally, we showed that the photocycle of active LiCre is faster than the one of active nMag/pMag split Cre.
evidence: The discussion summarizes comparative data from the experiments on periodic stimulation.

claim: The faster photocycle of LiCre offers higher temporal precision for the induction of recombination.
source: This offers higher temporal precision for the induction of recombination.
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation of the faster photocycle property.

claim: Contacts between αA and αE helices associate all four amino-terminal domains of Cre.
source: Contacts between αA and αE associate all four amino-terminal domains (Figure 1a), and contacts involving αN lock the four carboxy-terminal domains in a cyclic manner (Figure 1b).
evidence: The results section describes structural features shown in Figure 1a based on PDB structure 1NZB.

claim: Contacts involving αN helix lock the four carboxy-terminal domains of Cre in a cyclic manner.
source: Contacts between αA and αE associate all four amino-terminal domains (Figure 1a), and contacts involving αN lock the four carboxy-terminal domains in a cyclic manner (Figure 1b).
evidence: The results section describes structural features shown in Figure 1b based on PDB structure 1NZB.

claim: Wild-type Cre protein activated GFP expression in all cells under the tested conditions.
source: As a control, we observed that the wild-type Cre protein activated GFP expression in all cells under these conditions.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1d showing wild-type Cre activity.

claim: Cre mutants lacking the last two or the last three carboxy-terminal residues displayed full activity.
source: Mutants lacking the last two or the last three carboxy-terminal residues displayed full activity.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1d on C-terminal deletion mutants.

claim: Helix αN is needed for Cre activity and its residue E340 is implicated.
source: Our series of mutants showed that helix αN is needed for activity and that its residue E340 (located at position −4 from the protein end) is implicated.
evidence: The results section interprets experimental data from Figure 1d on the role of helix αN.

claim: E340 of Cre interacts with residue R192 of the adjacent unit in the tetramer structure.
source: The role of this glutamic acid is most likely to stabilize the complex: the tetramer structure indicates that it interacts with residue R192 of the adjacent unit (Figure 1e).
evidence: The results section describes structural interactions shown in Figure 1e based on PDB structure 1NZB.

claim: D341 of Cre forms salt bridges with R139 that probably reinforce attraction between two protein units.
source: Interestingly, although D341 was not essential for activity, the salt bridges of this residue with R139 probably also reinforce attraction between the two protein units.
evidence: The results section interprets structural data and experimental observations.

claim: The free-energy barrier for displacing the αN helix was much lower if E340 and D341 were replaced by alanines.
source: Biomolecular simulations using a simplistic force-field model showed that the free-energy barrier for displacing the αN helix was much lower if E340 and D341 were replaced by alanines (Figure 1f).
evidence: The results section reports computational simulation data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–21 of Cre (immediately upstream of helix A) had no effect when the C-terminus was wild-type.
source: When the C-terminus was wild-type, removing residues 2–21 (immediately upstream of helix A) had no effect and removing residues 2–28 (partial truncation of αA) decreased the activity by ~10%.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1g on N-terminal deletions.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–28 of Cre (partial truncation of αA) decreased the activity by approximately 10% when the C-terminus was wild-type.
source: When the C-terminus was wild-type, removing residues 2–21 (immediately upstream of helix A) had no effect and removing residues 2–28 (partial truncation of αA) decreased the activity by ~10%.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1g on N-terminal deletions.

claim: When the C-terminus contained the E340A D341A mutation, deletion of residues 2–21 reduced Cre activity by 12%.
source: When the C-terminus contained the E340A D341A mutation, deletions 2–21 and 2–28 were much more severe, reducing the activity by 12% and 80%, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1g on combined N-terminal and C-terminal mutations.

claim: When the C-terminus contained the E340A D341A mutation, deletion of residues 2–28 reduced Cre activity by 80%.
source: When the C-terminus contained the E340A D341A mutation, deletions 2–21 and 2–28 were much more severe, reducing the activity by 12% and 80%, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 1g on combined N-terminal and C-terminal mutations.

claim: There are genetic interactions between the N-terminal and C-terminal extremities of Cre protein.
source: This revealed genetic interactions between the extremities of the protein, which is fully consistent with a cooperative role of helices αA and αN in stabilizing an active tetramer complex.
evidence: The results section interprets experimental data from Figure 1g showing different effects of N-terminal deletions depending on C-terminal context.

claim: Helices αA and αN have a cooperative role in stabilizing an active Cre tetramer complex.
source: This revealed genetic interactions between the extremities of the protein, which is fully consistent with a cooperative role of helices αA and αN in stabilizing an active tetramer complex.
evidence: The results section interprets experimental data from Figure 1g on genetic interactions.

claim: The chimeric protein containing full-length Cre connected to VVD via four amino acids did not display light-dependent recombinase activity.
source: The resulting chimeric protein, which contained the full-length Cre connected to VVD via four amino acids, did not display light-dependent recombinase activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 on Cre-VVD fusions.

claim: Introducing the E340A D341A double mutation in the Cre-VVD chimeric protein reduced the overall activity but did not cause light dependency.
source: Introducing the (E340A D341A) double mutation in this chimeric protein reduced the overall activity – as expected from above – but did not cause light dependency.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 on mutant Cre-VVD fusions.

claim: The activity of Cre mutants E340R D341A and E340R D341R was markedly reduced, probably because attraction between E340 and R192 was changed into repulsion between two positively charged arginines.
source: We noted, however, that the activity of mutants (E340R D341A) and (E340R D341R) was markedly reduced, probably because attraction between E340 and R192 was changed into repulsion between two positively charged arginines.
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and provides an interpretation.

claim: Four constructs corresponding to fusions of AsLOV2 to residues 17, 19, 27, and 32 of Cre showed higher activity after light stimulation.
source: Although variability was high between independent transformants, we identified four constructs – corresponding to fusions of AsLOV2 to residues 17, 19, 27, and 32 of Cre, respectively – where the assay indicated a higher activity after light stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplement 2 on AsLOV2-Cre fusions.

claim: Fusion positions 19, 27, and 32 of AsLOV2 to Cre showed differential activity between dark and light conditions after validation.
source: This validated a differential activity between dark and light conditions for the constructs corresponding to fusion positions 19, 27, and 32 (Figure 2a).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2a validating light-dependent activity.

claim: An isoleucine insertion at the junction position of LOV_Cre32 achieved the strongest reduction in residual activity.
source: For the other five clones, residual activity was indeed reduced compared to LOV_Cre32, with the strongest reduction being achieved by an isoleucine insertion at the junction position (Figure 2b, clone v).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2b on junction mutagenesis.

claim: The improvement in reduced residual activity by isoleucine insertion was accompanied by a weaker induced activity and a larger variability between independent assays.
source: However, this improvement was also accompanied by a weaker induced activity and a larger variability between independent assays.
evidence: The results section reports experimental observations from Figure 2b on the trade-offs of junction mutagenesis.

claim: Fusion of AsLOV2 at position 20 of the Cre A340A341 double mutant conferred light-dependent activity.
source: This revealed that fusion at position 20, but not 21 or 22, conferred light-dependent activity (Figure 2c).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 2c on AsLOV2 fusions to Cre A340A341 mutant.

claim: The LiCre construct includes an A->D mutation at the fusion junction.
source: Sequencing revealed that it also included a A->D mutation at the fusion junction (Supplementary file 1 – Supplementary Text S2).
evidence: The results section reports sequencing data revealing an additional mutation in LiCre.

claim: The highest activity of LiCre (approximately 65% of switched cells) was obtained with 90 min illumination at 36.3 mW/cm2.
source: The highest activity (~65% of switched cells) was obtained with 90 min illumination at 36.3 mW/cm2 (Figure 3a).
evidence: The results section reports experimental data from Figure 3a on LiCre photoactivation conditions.

claim: The minimal light intensity required for LiCre stimulation was between 0.057 and 1.815 mW/cm2.
